title: ITA Section 37(1.2): SR&ED Expenditure Timing Rules
description: Master ITA Section 37(1.2) legislation on SR&ED expenditure timing in Canada. Find out when R&D expenses are deemed incurred for your Canadian tax claim.
summary: This page explains SR&ED expenditure timing under section 37 of Canada's Income Tax Act for taxpayers carrying on business in Canada. Pooled current and eligible capital SR&ED expenditures may be deducted in the year incurred or carried forward indefinitely, but remuneration unpaid 180 days after year-end is deemed not incurred, and corporations must file within 18 months of year-end.

body.text: This page explains SR&ED expenditure timing under section 37 of Canada's Income Tax Act for taxpayers carrying on business in Canada. Pooled current and eligible capital SR&ED expenditures may be deducted in the year incurred or carried forward indefinitely, but remuneration unpaid 180 days after year-end is deemed not incurred, and corporations must file within 18 months of year-end.
Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture

Canada operates one of the most mature and financially significant research and development tax incentive frameworks in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) in conjunction with tax policy formulated by the Department of Finance Canada, the SR&ED regime delivers statutory tax relief through a dual mechanism under the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)). First, subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct 100% of current and eligible capital SR&ED expenditures in the taxation year incurred or to carry those pooled expenditures forward indefinitely to offset future business income. Second, Sections 127 and 127.1 provide a federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a 15% basic rate for general corporate claimants to an enhanced 35% refundable rate for qualifying small and medium-sized innovative corporations.

The legislative landscape governing Canadian R&D incentives underwent its most consequential structural modernization in over a decade with the enactment of Bill C-15, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. From 2014 through late 2024, Canada's federal SR&ED architecture had remained largely static: the enhanced 35% expenditure limit was frozen at $3,000,000, capital expenditures were entirely excluded from the program, public corporations were categorically barred from the enhanced refundable credit regardless of size, and the expenditure limit phased out rapidly between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada. That legacy structure penalized capital-intensive technology companies—particularly in clean technology, biotechnology, semiconductor manufacturing, and artificial intelligence hardware—whose balance sheets accumulated substantial debt or equity financing prior to commercial revenue generation.

Applying retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 fundamentally recalibrated the federal incentive architecture across five interconnected statutory dimensions. First, Parliament doubled the annual expenditure threshold eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, thereby raising the maximum annual refundable federal cash credit on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Second, access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC—historically restricted to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) as defined in subsection 125(7)—was extended to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under subsections 127(9) and 127(10.6), eliminating the "going-public penalty" that previously stripped emerging Canadian technology firms of refundable R&D support upon listing on a domestic or foreign stock exchange. Third, for CCPCs utilizing the default capital-based phase-out under amended subsection 127(10.2), the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada thresholds expanded from the legacy $10,000,000–$50,000,000 corridor to a widened $15,000,000–$75,000,000 corridor. Fourth, to prevent asset-heavy innovators from prematurely losing access to the 35% credit due to balance-sheet capitalization, Parliament enacted a three-year average annual gross revenue phase-out alternative spanning $15,000,000 to $75,000,000, which applies mandatorily to ECPCs under subsection 127(10.6) and by formal election to single or associated CCPCs under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32). Fifth, reversing the 2014 repeal of capital costs, Bill C-15 restored SR&ED eligibility for new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, for use all or substantially all (90% or more) in SR&ED in Canada, allowing such assets to enter both the Section 37 deduction pool and the federal ITC base with a 40% refundability rate on enhanced ITCs.

Concurrently, at the provincial level, the Quebec 2025–2026 Budget, tabled on March 25, 2025, executed a sweeping consolidation of provincial R&D fiscal measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. By abolishing six fragmented legacy R&D and industrial design tax credits and replacing them with the unified, refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)—which provides a 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D, pre-commercialization, and capital expenditures above a statutory exclusion threshold, and 20% on the excess—Quebec aligned its provincial regime with the restored federal capital rules while expanding eligible activities into late-stage technological validation and prototyping. Together with the CRA's introduction of an elective pre-claim technical approval process and artificial intelligence audit triage on April 1, 2026, these legislative reforms shift Canada's R&D tax regime toward higher capital intensity, broader public-market accessibility, and accelerated administrative certainty.

body.text: Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Technical Eligibility Criteria
Analysis of Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Aligned structurally with the international standards of the OECD Frascati Manual, subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Rather than evaluating eligibility through industry-specific classifications or commercial outcomes, the statute bifurcates eligible work into three foundational scientific or technological pillars under paragraphs 248(1)(a), (b), and (c), supplemented by one category of commensurate support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) and bounded by seven explicit statutory exclusions under paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k).

Under paragraph 248(1)(a), basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, typically conducted in foundational physics, chemistry, biology, or theoretical computer science. Under paragraph 248(1)(b), applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Because applied research and experimental development share the characteristic of having a practical commercial or industrial application in view, the CRA's administrative guidelines apply parallel analytical criteria to both branches. The third and predominant pillar, experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c), covers work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In practice, experimental development accounts for the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada because it explicitly embraces incremental technological advancements in industrial engineering, manufacturing processes, and software architectures.

Once a taxpayer establishes the existence of basic research, applied research, or experimental development under paragraphs (a) through (c), paragraph 248(1)(d) extends eligibility to derivative support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer that is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of that core SR&ED work carried on in Canada. Crucially, paragraph 248(1)(d) is an exhaustive statutory list: support work is eligible only if it falls within one of eight enumerated technical categories—namely engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research. Any ancillary corporate activity that falls outside those eight specified categories is statutorily ineligible as support work, even if it indirectly facilitates an R&D project.
Statutory Exclusions Under Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)

Even where a corporate initiative involves scientific inquiry or product engineering, subsection 248(1) explicitly carves out seven categories of commercial, routine, or non-scientific activity that cannot be claimed as SR&ED. Specifically, paragraph (e) excludes market research or sales promotion; paragraph (f) excludes quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; paragraph (g) excludes research in the social sciences or the humanities; paragraph (h) excludes prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; paragraph (i) excludes the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; paragraph (j) excludes style changes; and paragraph (k) excludes routine data collection.

body.text: A sophisticated legal and audit distinction governs the boundary between eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) and excluded work under paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k). In CRA administrative policy, statutory exclusions are evaluated only after the reviewer has verified that eligible core SR&ED work has been performed, and the determinative criterion separating eligible support work (such as "data collection" or "testing" under paragraph (d)) from excluded work (such as "routine data collection" under paragraph (k) or "routine testing" under paragraph (f)) is the purpose for which the activity was performed. When data collection or testing is carried out specifically and exclusively to test a scientific hypothesis or resolve a technological uncertainty within an active SR&ED investigation, it qualifies as commensurate support work under paragraph 248(1)(d). Conversely, if the exact same technical testing protocol or data gathering is executed for commercial quality assurance, user acceptance, or regulatory compliance after the underlying technological uncertainty has been resolved, it is barred under paragraphs (f), (i), or (k). Similarly, in Canada's resource extraction industries, while prospecting, exploring, or drilling for minerals, petroleum, or natural gas is statutorily excluded under paragraph 248(1)(h), a resource company that simultaneously conducts experimental development on novel metallurgical extraction processes or downhole drilling telemetry can claim the eligible experimental development work, provided all prospecting and mineral exploration costs are rigorously segregated and excluded.
The CRA "Why" and "How" Requirements and the Three-Part Eligibility Test

In the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, the statutory language of subsection 248(1) is synthesized into two overarching operational mandates—Why the work was conducted and How the work was conducted—which are enforced during technical audits through the CRA's mandatory Three-Part Eligibility Test. Every claimed project is audited against all three criteria independently by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), and failure to satisfy any single criterion results in the complete disqualification of the project.

The first criterion, Technological Uncertainty, addresses the "Why" mandate by requiring the claimant to prove that the desired technological objective or problem could not be resolved using standard practice, routine engineering, publicly available literature, or the baseline knowledge of competent professionals in the relevant field. Technological uncertainty arises either from a fundamental gap in existing scientific knowledge or from system uncertainty, where known components, algorithms, or physical subsystems interact in unpredictable ways when integrated into a constrained or high-scale architecture—such as attempting to engineer a software data pipeline capable of processing 10 million events per second with sub-100-millisecond latency on commodity hardware where established algorithms fail at that throughput. In evaluating this first gate, the CRA enforces an absolute separation between technological uncertainty and commercial or business uncertainty: not knowing whether customers will adopt a product, whether a feature set will achieve market fit, or whether a project can be delivered on budget is a commercial question that fails the statutory test. Moreover, the CRA guidelines explicitly stipulate that acquiring existing knowledge or know-how—whether through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or external consultants, or purchasing proprietary technology—does not constitute attempting to resolve technological uncertainty.

The second criterion, Systematic Investigation or Search, addresses the "How" mandate by requiring the claimant to demonstrate that it followed a structured scientific method to overcome the identified technological uncertainty. Under CRA policy, a systematic investigation requires four sequential operational steps: generating an explicit idea or hypothesis consistent with known scientific or technological facts to serve as the starting point for investigation; testing that idea or hypothesis by means of planned experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve across iterative test cycles; developing logical conclusions grounded in the measured results or findings of the experiments; and maintaining contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses. Ad hoc troubleshooting, intuition-based code refactoring, or undocumented "trial and error" lacks the scientific rigour of hypothesis testing and is systematically denied upon audit.

The third criterion, Technological Advancement, requires that the systematic investigation be undertaken for the purpose of generating new scientific or technological knowledge or capabilities that advance the existing state of the art. The advancement need not be a disruptive industry breakthrough; incremental advancements—such as formulating a novel caching strategy that reduces query latency for a specific class of complex database operations from over 15 seconds to sub-second response times—fully satisfy subsection 248(1). A foundational principle of Canadian SR&ED law is that both successful and failed projects qualify for tax incentives. Because eligibility turns on the scientific or technological nature of the investigation attempted rather than commercial success, an experiment that conclusively falsifies a hypothesis and proves that a proposed technological pathway cannot work under specified constraints advances the technological knowledge base and is 100% eligible.
Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Rates, Caps, and Phase-Out Mechanics
Federal ITC Rate Structure and Refundability Matrix

Under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, the rate at which a claimant earns federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits and the percentage of those credits that can be refunded in cash depend on four statutory variables: the legal classification of the taxpayer (CCPC, ECPC, other corporation, individual proprietorship, trust, or partnership member); whether the claimant's qualified expenditures fall within or exceed its annual expenditure limit; whether the underlying expenditures are current expenditures (including the Prescribed Proxy Amount) or capital expenditures; and whether a CCPC is categorized as a "qualifying corporation" or an "excluded corporation".

Across all taxpayer classes, the basic federal ITC rate is 15% of the excess of a claimant's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool over the total of all provincial super-allowance benefit amounts at the end of the taxation year. Under subsection 127(10.1), CCPCs and—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn an additional 20% enhancement on top of the 15% basic rate, producing the 35% enhanced ITC rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit of $6,000,000. Any qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in the current taxation year that exceed the corporation's allocated expenditure limit earn the ITC at the basic 15% rate. Furthermore, if a claimant received government or non-government assistance or a contract payment in a previous taxation year that is repaid or adjusted, or receives assistance in the current year, that assistance reduces the qualified expenditure pool eligible for the 35% enhanced rate.

With respect to cash refundability under Section 127.1, qualifying CCPCs (that are not excluded corporations) and ECPCs (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) receive a 100% cash refund of the unclaimed balance of the 35% enhanced ITC earned on current SR&ED expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), and a 40% cash refund of the unclaimed balance of the 35% enhanced ITC earned on newly eligible capital expenditures. For expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 expenditure limit (which earn the 15% basic rate), a CCPC that is a "qualifying corporation" receives a 40% cash refund on both current and capital expenditures over the limit, whereas an ECPC or a CCPC that is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation receives 0% refundability above the expenditure limit. Conversely, a CCPC that is a qualifying corporation but is also classified as an "excluded corporation" receives a reduced 40% refund rate across all tiers (both up to and over the expenditure limit, on both current and capital expenditures). Unincorporated individuals (sole proprietorships), qualifying trusts (where each beneficiary is an individual or a qualifying corporation), and members of a partnership earn the basic 15% ITC rate on all qualified expenditures and are entitled to a 40% cash refund on both current and capital expenditures. All other corporations—including foreign-controlled subsidiaries, non-eligible public corporations, and CCPCs or ECPCs whose expenditure limit has phased out and that do not qualify for the 40% refund tier—earn a 15% non-refundable ITC.

body.text: Legacy CCPC Expenditure Limit Formula (Taxation Years Beginning Before December 16, 2024)

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, a CCPC's $3,000,000 maximum expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2) was reduced solely by reference to the taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under section 181.2 for general corporations, section 181.3 for financial institutions, or section 181.4 for non-residents) of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs for the immediately preceding taxation year. Once the preceding year's combined taxable capital reached $10,000,000, the expenditure limit decreased linearly until it was eliminated entirely at $50,000,000:

where TC<sub>prior</sub> denotes the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated corporations for the prior taxation year, bounded such that whenever TC<sub>prior</sub> ≥ $50,000,000, the expenditure limit equals $0.
Current CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024)

Under amended subsection 127(10.2), for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC that uses the default taxable capital method retains the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit until its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (combined across all CCPCs in an associated group) reaches $15,000,000, above which the limit phases out linearly over a $60,000,000 span until becoming nil ($0) at $75,000,000:
Expenditure Limit<sub>CCPC Capital</sub> = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − max(0, TC<sub>prior</sub> − $15,000,000)) ÷ $60,000,000

Mathematically, every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada in excess of $15,000,000 reduces the CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1. Because venture-backed startups raising Series B or Series C equity rounds or project debt frequently cross $15,000,000 in paid-up capital and debt long before achieving commercial profitability, relying passively on the default taxable capital formula can severely erode refundable SR&ED entitlements.
ECPC and Electing CCPC Revenue Phase-Out Formula (Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024)

To decouple SR&ED eligibility from balance-sheet capitalization, subsection 127(10.6) establishes a revenue-based phase-out method for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations, while subsections 127(10.31) (for a single unassociated CCPC) and 127(10.32) (for a CCPC having associated corporations) permit CCPCs to elect on a prescribed form to calculate their expenditure limit using the identical revenue-based formula. Under this Revenue Method, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced based on the corporation's (or group's) average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (Rev3yr), phasing out begins at $15,000,000, and the expenditure limit becomes nil ($0) when three-year average annual revenue reaches $75,000,000 or greater:
Expenditure Limit<sub>Revenue Method</sub> = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − max(0, Rev<sub>3yr</sub> − $15,000,000)) ÷ $60,000,000

The statutory architecture governing the Revenue Method enforces rigorous group-wide aggregation rules to prevent artificial revenue splitting across corporate structures. For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations, subsection 127(10.62) mandates that where an ECPC is a member of a consolidated group that prepares consolidated financial statements (defined in subsection 233.8(1) as financial statements presenting the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the group members as a single economic entity), the single $6,000,000 expenditure limit is shared among all members of the consolidated group. The annual revenue reflected in the group's consolidated financial statements over the three preceding fiscal years is used to calculate the average annual revenue and the resulting expenditure limit; if an entity joins or leaves the consolidated group during the taxation year, the average annual revenue used is that of the consolidated group as reflected in the consolidated financial statements for the taxation year in question.

Similarly, where a CCPC belongs to a group of associated corporations, subsection 127(10.32) prohibits cherry-picking between the capital and revenue methods within the same corporate family: all CCPCs in the associated group must jointly elect to use the Revenue Method and must allocate the resulting expenditure limit among the group members using the prescribed form. In computing the associated group's three-year average annual revenue, the group is required to sum the average annual revenue amounts reflected in the financial statements of every member corporation of the group for the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether those corporations were associated during the entirety of that three-year look-back period. Furthermore, the calculation must include each corporation's reasonable share of annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of any partnership or trust in which the corporation held an interest, while permitting reasonable eliminations and adjustments—such as removing intra-group sales of goods or services—so that the associated group's annual revenue accurately reflects a single economic entity. Finally, under subsection 127(10.61) and CRA policy, if an ECPC or an electing CCPC has been in existence for fewer than three preceding fiscal years, its average annual revenue must be calculated based on the actual number of fiscal years available, with analogous proration adjustments applied where any of those preceding fiscal years was a short taxation year.
Associated Corporations, Short Taxation Years, and Multiple Year-Ends

Where CCPCs are associated with one another under Section 256 (or ECPCs are members of a consolidated group), the group must file an agreement on a prescribed form—specifically Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.3)—to allocate the group's single annual expenditure limit among its constituent corporations. Ignoring association rules is a frequent and costly compliance failure: under subsection 127(10.4), if an associated group fails to file its allocation agreement within 30 days after receiving written notice from the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister will allocate the group's expenditure limit among one or more of the associated corporations, removing the group's ability to choose its own allocation for that year. (Relief from association for SR&ED purposes is available only in narrow circumstances where corporations satisfy the statutory conditions for deemed non-association under subsections 127(10.22) and 127(10.23), paired with subsection 127.1(2.2)).

Under subsection 127(10.5) of the Income Tax Act, two specialized statutory rules govern corporations that experience short taxation years (fewer than 51 weeks) or multiple taxation years ending within the same calendar year. First, whenever a corporation has a short taxation year, its allocated expenditure limit must be prorated based on the exact ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365 days:
Prorated Expenditure Limit = Allocated Expenditure Limit × (Days in Short Taxation Year ÷ 365)

Second, specific anti-duplication rules apply under subsection 127(10.5) if a CCPC (the first corporation) has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC that has a taxation year ending in that same calendar year. In that scenario, the expenditure limit of the first corporation for each subsequent taxation year ending in that calendar year is equal to the expenditure limit allocated to it for its first taxation year ending in that calendar year, prorated by the number of days in the subsequent short taxation year divided by 365. To illustrate this mechanism using the CRA's official policy example, suppose Corporation P and Corporation Q are associated CCPCs that share a $6,000,000 group expenditure limit and allocate it equally ($3,000,000 to each corporation) between Corporation P's June 30, 2027 taxation year-end and Corporation Q's December 31, 2027 taxation year-end. If Corporation P subsequently undergoes a corporate reorganization or year-end change resulting in a second taxation year ending on December 31, 2027 (spanning 184 days from July 1 to December 31, 2027), Corporation P's expenditure limit for its December 31, 2027 taxation year is determined under subsection 127(10.5) by prorating its June 30, 2027 allocation: $3,000,000 × (184 days ÷ 365 days) = $1,512,328.
Carryover Provisions and Taxability of ITCs

When a corporation earns non-refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credits at the 15% basic rate (or earns partially non-refundable credits on capital expenditures, or elects not to receive a cash refund) in excess of its federal Part I income tax payable for the taxation year, the unused ITC balance does not expire at year-end. Instead, unused SR&ED ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years to recover prior federal Part I taxes paid and carried forward for up to 20 taxation years to shelter future federal income tax liabilities.

In financial modelling, corporate tax planners must account for the statutory taxability of SR&ED credits. Any federal SR&ED ITC claimed in a taxation year—whether applied as an offset against Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund under Section 127.1—reduces the taxpayer's Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year (and to the extent that reduction drives the Section 37 pool negative at the end of that following year, the negative balance is included directly in the taxpayer's taxable business income). Consequently, used and refunded federal SR&ED tax credits are effectively subject to corporate income tax in the taxation year following the year in which they are claimed or refunded.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Overhead Calculation Methods

To qualify for inclusion in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool, an expenditure must be incurred by the claimant for SR&ED carried on in Canada, must relate to a business carried on by the claimant, and must be reasonable in the circumstances under Section 67 of the Income Tax Act.
Salaries and Wages: Direct Engagement, Unpaid Amounts, and Specified Employees

Under the definition of "salary or wages" in subsection 248(1) and the SR&ED pooling provisions of subsection 37(8), eligible labour expenditures consist of the income of an employee from an office or employment as computed under Subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Income Tax Act (plus the employer's share of Canada Pension Plan [CPP], Québec Pension Plan [QPP], Employment Insurance [EI], Québec Parental Insurance Plan [QPIP], and provincial workers' compensation board assessments when using the traditional overhead method) paid to employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

In auditing payroll claims under the CRA's Salary or Wages Policy, reviewers enforce four primary statutory and administrative rules. First, whether an employee is "directly engaged" in SR&ED is determined strictly by the hands-on technical tasks performed by the individual and never by the employee's corporate job title or organizational department. Directly engaged activities encompass hands-on scientific experimentation, engineering analysis, eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support tasks (such as writing experimental code or executing benchmark tests), and first-line technical direction of SR&ED staff, whereas general executive management, human resources, finance, legal, and administrative support are excluded from direct labour. Second, several categories of employment compensation are statutorily deemed not to be incurred or are excluded from SR&ED wages: the value of non-cash taxable benefits, employee stock option benefits under Section 7, and any Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) or Provincial Sales Tax (PST) embedded in taxable benefits on an employee's T4 slip for which the employer claims an Input Tax Credit (ITC) or provincial rebate. Under subsection 248(16) of the Income Tax Act, any GST/HST input tax credit or provincial sales tax rebate that can be claimed by the employer is deemed to be government assistance; therefore, no recoverable GST/HST or PST component may be included in allowable SR&ED salary or wages.

Third, subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act imposes a strict cash-settlement deadline on accrued compensation: any salary, wages, or other employee remuneration accrued at the end of a taxation year that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year. Fourth, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose stringent anti-avoidance caps on "specified employees"—defined in subsection 248(1) as employees who do not deal at arm's length with the employer or who are "specified shareholders" owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of any related corporation. Under paragraph 37(9)(a), a specified employee's deductible SR&ED remuneration cannot include any bonus or remuneration based on profits, and under subsection 37(9.1) the total deductible SR&ED salary for a specified employee is capped at five times (5x) the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual was employed by the corporation. Furthermore, when the claimant elects the Proxy Method to compute overhead, subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Income Tax Regulations restrict the specified employee's salary base for the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) to the lesser of: (i) actual base salary (excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits) multiplied by the percentage of time directly engaged in SR&ED, subject to a hard ceiling of 75% of total working time; and (ii) 2.5 times (2.5x) the YMPE, prorated for the number of days employed in the taxation year:
PPA Salary Base<sub>Specified Employee</sub> = min(Base Salary × min(%SR&ED Time, 0.75), 2.5 × YMPE)

(Note: Associated corporations that employ the same specified employee must allocate these 5 × YMPE and 2.5 × YMPE ceilings among themselves so that the individual is not double-counted across the corporate group).
Overhead Allocation: The Proxy Method vs. The Traditional Method

A taxpayer claiming SR&ED in Canada must elect on Form T661 for each taxation year whether to account for SR&ED overhead and other indirect expenditures using the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method; once the return is filed for a taxation year, the chosen method is irrevocable for that year.

Under the Proxy Method, governed by subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the claimant does not itemize actual overhead costs on Form T661. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base. In auditing corporate claims, a recurring technical error in outdated secondary literature is the assertion that the proxy rate is 65%: historically, the PPA rate was 65% up to 2012, transitioned to 60% for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 2014 under Regulation 2900(4). Two structural features define the PPA: first, because the PPA is a purely notional figure, it does not enter the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (rather, the taxpayer simply deducts its actual business overhead expenses under ordinary Part I rules in Sections 9 and 18), but 100% of the PPA enters the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool to earn the 35% or 15% federal ITC and 100% refundability. Second, the salary base to which the 55% factor applies is narrower than the Section 37 deductible salary pool: for all employees (both arm's-length and specified), the PPA salary base excludes taxable benefits, bonuses, and remuneration based on profits, plus the employer's share of payroll taxes, and applies the 2.5 × YMPE and 75% time caps to specified employees under Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8).

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, governed by subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations, the claimant foregoes the 55% PPA and instead claims actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly attributable (and incremental) to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. While the Traditional Method can yield a higher tax credit for heavy industrial or manufacturing R&D facilities where dedicated factory utilities, shop supplies, and non-salaried support costs exceed 55% of direct R&D payroll, it imposes an onerous record-keeping and audit burden, requiring the taxpayer to substantiate every individual invoice and allocation formula during a CRA financial review. For software, data analytics, biotechnology, and engineering design enterprises where labour is the dominant cost driver, the Proxy Method is overwhelmingly preferred because salary records and timesheets drive the entire overhead calculation.

body.text: Materials Consumed or Transformed

Under subsection 37(1) and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations, a claimant may claim 100% of the cost of materials that are consumed (destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during experimental runs) or transformed (incorporated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom experimental assembly) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Eligible material costs include raw chemicals, electronic components, assay reagents, and testing supplies physically expended during experimentation. If an experimental prototype or transformed material is later sold commercially or converted to commercial production use, the Income Tax Act enforces SR&ED recapture rules to claw back the lesser of the fair market value or proceeds of disposition and the original material cost claimed in the SR&ED pool.
Cloud Computing, Software, and Data Infrastructure Costs

With the proliferation of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and cloud-native software engineering, cloud computing expenditures represent a major focal point in contemporary CRA audits. Under current CRA administrative guidance, cloud computing costs—specifically Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) and Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) compute instances, elastic GPU/TPU clusters used to train experimental neural networks, and dedicated sandboxed development environments on Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), or Microsoft Azure—used directly and exclusively for eligible SR&ED activities qualify for SR&ED as materials consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED (or as directly attributable SR&ED expenditures). Conversely, the acquisition of off-the-shelf commercial software licences and general intellectual property rights used in R&D is statutorily non-eligible.

To survive a CRA financial audit of cloud computing expenses, software and SaaS claimants must enforce a strict accounting separation between production infrastructure and experimental R&D infrastructure. Cloud servers and third-party APIs that host live commercial applications for paying customers belong in Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) / Cost of Revenue, and staging environments used for routine quality assurance, load testing under known parameters, or general corporate operations are 100% ineligible for SR&ED. Coding all AWS, GCP, Azure, and third-party API invoices into a single "Software Subscriptions" or "Hosting" general ledger account is one of the most common bookkeeping errors among Canadian technology companies, distorting both SaaS gross margins (which typically target 65%–80%) and disqualifying SR&ED claims for lack of specific attribution. Best-practice compliance requires configuring separate cloud billing accounts or applying granular automated resource tags in AWS, GCP, and Azure that map specific compute clusters directly to SR&ED project codes, exporting those tagged cost reports monthly into an SR&ED-aware chart of accounts. Furthermore, because provinces including British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba have enacted specific Provincial Sales Tax (PST) rules taxing SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS cloud services purchased or used within their jurisdictions, claimants must map the geographic location of R&D personnel and related cloud infrastructure, implement tax proration where necessary, and strip any recoverable GST/HST or provincial input tax credits from the SR&ED claim base under subsection 248(16).
Subcontractors and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant outsources R&D tasks to external parties, the Income Tax Act differentiates sharply between arm's-length subcontractors, non-arm's-length subcontractors, and third-party research institutions. An arm's-length SR&ED contract is a contract under which an independent contractor performs basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work in Canada on behalf of the claimant. While 100% of an eligible arm's-length contract payment is deductible in the Section 37 expenditure pool, only 80% of the eligible contract expenditure is included in the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for calculating the 35% or 15% federal ITC. This statutory 20% reduction removes the contractor's assumed profit margin so that the federal tax credit subsidizes only the underlying R&D cost. Crucially, all subcontracted SR&ED work must be performed physically within Canada; any portion of a subcontract performed outside Canada (offshore) is 100% ineligible for Canadian SR&ED incentives.

Where the subcontractor does not deal at arm's length with the claimant (for example, an affiliated or sister corporation controlled by the same parent company or shareholder group), the contract payment itself is excluded from the claimant's qualified expenditures. Instead, through a statutory look-through mechanism, the claim is restricted to the non-arm's-length contractor's actual underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures (such as the contractor's direct Canadian R&D wages and materials), completely eliminating any inter-company profit markup. Finally, third-party payments—defined as payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D consortia for SR&ED carried out in Canada that is related to a business class of the claimant, provided the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED—are included in the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool at the 80% inclusion rate.
Restored Capital Expenditures and Parallel CCA Accelerated Depreciation Regimes

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures (including capital expenditures deemed to have been made before December 16, 2024, under the lay-off rule) were completely excluded from the SR&ED program. Under Bill C-15, capital expenditures for new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, are once again eligible for both the Section 37 deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) SR&ED Investment Tax Credit. To qualify under the restored capital rules, the depreciable property must be acquired for use all or substantially all (defined as 90% or more of its operating time over its useful life) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or its value must be all or substantially all consumed in SR&ED in Canada. Land, buildings (other than a prescribed leasehold interest in a building), goodwill, and inventory remain statutorily excluded from the restored SR&ED capital regime. When a qualifying CCPC or ECPC claims eligible capital expenditures within its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, those capital expenditures earn the 35% enhanced ITC rate, and the unclaimed balance of that ITC is refundable in cash at a 40% refund rate (yielding an immediate 14% cash refund, i.e., 35% × 40%, with the remaining 21% credit offsetting Part I tax payable or carrying forward for up to 20 years).

Even where capital hardware (such as multipurpose cloud servers, networking gear, or laboratory equipment used 60% for R&D and 40% for commercial operations) falls short of the strict 90% "all or substantially all" SR&ED threshold, corporate taxpayers can leverage highly generous parallel Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) accelerated depreciation incentives under Section 20(1)(a), Schedule II, and Regulation 1100 of the Income Tax Regulations as amended by Bill C-15. Specifically, while ordinary CCA rates are 55% declining-balance for Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment, servers, and systems software), 30% for Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment), and 25% for Class 44 (patents or rights to use patented information), any property in Class 44, Class 46, or Class 50 acquired after April 15, 2024, and available for use before 2027 qualifies for 100% immediate expensing in the year it becomes available for use, with the half-year rule completely suspended. (Taxpayers should note that Class 52 is a closed historical class that accepts no new asset additions, and that there is no minimum "over 50% business use" threshold for corporate CCA—capital cost allowance is simply claimed on the business-use proportion of the asset's cost). Furthermore, for broader classes of depreciable capital property that do not fall within Classes 44, 46, or 50, Bill C-15 introduced the Reinstated Accelerated Investment Incentive for property acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030, granting an enhanced first-year CCA deduction equal to 3 times (3x) the normal first-year amount (or 1.5× where the half-year rule would not normally apply), which steps down to 2 times (2x) (or 1.25×) for property becoming available for use between 2030 and 2033.

body.text: Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Stacking Mechanics
Government Assistance and Stacking Equation

Every Canadian province (as well as the Yukon Territory) administers a sub-national R&D tax credit or innovation grant that stacks atop the federal SR&ED program. In addition, Canadian innovators frequently receive direct non-dilutive R&D grants, most notably from the National Research Council of Canada's Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which reimburses a portion of technical salaries and contractor costs. While taxpayers are fully permitted to combine NRC IRAP grants, provincial R&D tax credits, and federal SR&ED tax credits on the same technology project, the Income Tax Act prevents double-dipping on the identical dollar of expenditure by classifying both provincial R&D tax credits and government grants as government assistance under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d).

Specifically, any government assistance or non-government assistance that a taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED at the time of filing its income tax return must be deducted from both the Section 37 expenditure pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool before the federal 35% or 15% SR&ED ITC is calculated. If a corporation incurs E in gross eligible SR&ED expenditures (including the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount where the proxy method is elected), receives GIRAP in NRC IRAP grant funding, and earns Cprov in provincial R&D or AI tax credits attributable to those SR&ED expenditures, the net federal SR&ED qualified expenditure base Efed and resulting federal credit are governed by the following stacking equations:
Efed = E − GIRAP − Cprov
Federal ITC = rfed × (E − GIRAP − Cprov)

where rfed ∈ {0.35, 0.15} represents the applicable federal SR&ED ITC rate. If the taxpayer subsequently repays any portion of that government assistance or contract payment in a later taxation year, the repaid amount is added back to the qualified expenditure pool in the year of repayment.
Quebec's 2025–2026 Overhaul: The Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

The most sweeping provincial R&D reform in recent Canadian fiscal history was enacted by the Government of Quebec in its 2025–2026 Budget (tabled March 25, 2025). To eliminate administrative fragmentation and redirect public subsidies toward high-impact R&D and commercialization, Quebec abolished six legacy tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025: the Tax credit for salaries (R&D); the Tax credit for university research and for research carried on by a public research centre or a research consortium; the Tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research; the Tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium; the Tax credit for technological adaptation services; and the industrial design component of the Tax credit for an in-house design activity (while preserving the fashion design component of that credit). Under transitional grandfathering rules, a taxpayer's or partnership's eligible fee balance at the end of a taxation year or fiscal period ending after March 25, 2025, can continue to generate the legacy research consortium tax credit under existing terms for taxation years ending on or before December 31, 2029. Moreover, despite abolishing the separate university and consortium credits, Quebec amended the Act respecting the sectoral parameters of certain fiscal measures so that the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy continues to issue recognition certificates for eligible public research centres and eligible research consortia for purposes of the new unified regime.

In place of the six repealed incentives, Quebec created the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which applies to taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, and is claimed on Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR (with associated corporations allocating the $1,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit on Form RD-1029.8.EN) alongside the Quebec CO-17 corporate income tax return. Unlike unincorporated proprietorships, only corporations that carry on a business in Quebec, maintain an establishment in Quebec, perform eligible activities in Quebec (or have them performed on their behalf in Quebec under contract), and are not excluded corporations qualify for the CRIC.
Core Structural Parameters of the Quebec CRIC
The CRIC modernizes Quebec's innovation support across four foundational parameters:

First, the CRIC expands the scope of eligible technical activities beyond traditional R&D. While federal SR&ED eligibility terminates the moment technological uncertainty is resolved, the CRIC covers both traditional scientific research and experimental development carried out in Quebec and pre-commercialization activities performed in Quebec as a direct continuation of R&D—specifically encompassing technological validation, product testing, regulatory certification trials, and pre-production prototyping.

Second, the CRIC standardizes eligible expenditure categories and aligns with federal capital restoration. Eligible CRIC expenditures encompass: 100% of wages paid to employees directly engaged in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Quebec (including directly related support roles); a standardized 50% of eligible subcontracting contracts executed in Quebec, regardless of whether the subcontractor is an arm's-length private R&D contractor, a university, a College Centre for the Transfer of Technology (CCTT), a public research centre, or a research consortium; and 100% of capital expenditures (CAPEX) on new depreciable equipment acquired and used almost exclusively (90% or more) in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Quebec. Capital property is considered incurred when it becomes available for use, must not have been previously used, must not be used as part of a large investment project benefiting from a tax holiday, and strictly excludes land, buildings, or rights in a building.

Third, the CRIC replaces the complex per-employee bi-annual thresholds of the former R&D salary credit with a unified CRIC Exclusion Threshold. For each taxation year, a corporation's net eligible CRIC expenditures must exceed an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of: (i) $50,000 (prorated for the number of days in the taxation year if the taxation year is shorter than 51 weeks); or (ii) the sum of the individual "employee thresholds" for all eligible employees, where each employee's threshold equals the basic personal amount applicable to Quebec personal income tax for the calendar year in which the corporation's taxation year begins, adjusted in proportion to the percentage of working time spent by that employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities.
Fourth, once net eligible expenditures exceed the applicable exclusion threshold, the CRIC provides a 100% refundable two-tier tax credit:

items: A 30% enhanced refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures in excess of the exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN); and
A 20% base refundable rate on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 enhanced limit.

Strategic Coordination with Other Quebec Innovation Incentives (CDAE-IA, DICI, and C3i)
To maximize total cash recovery in Quebec, corporate tax directors must coordinate the CRIC and federal SR&ED with three parallel Quebec fiscal instruments modified in the 2025–2026 Budget:

First, the Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (TCEB / CDAE) was overhauled for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, into the CDAE-IA, requiring that an employee's eligible e-business activities be connected to a project, mandate, or product that significantly integrates artificial intelligence (AI) functionalities. Routine maintenance or evolution of legacy information systems or technological infrastructure is no longer eligible, whereas data processing and hosting activities were added to the services criteria (with credit reductions in certain inter-company outsourcing cases). For the 2026 calendar year, CDAE-IA provides a 30% total credit (22% refundable + 8% non-refundable) on eligible technical salaries exceeding an exclusion threshold of $18,571 per eligible employee (with rates scheduled to adjust through 2028). Because CDAE-IA provides a high effective rate on AI-specialized salaries without consuming the $6,000,000 federal SR&ED expenditure limit—and remains available even after a company scales past $75,000,000 in capital or revenue—optimal stacking claims CDAE-IA first on AI/ML engineers and layers federal SR&ED (and CRIC) on broader non-AI software development, newly eligible capital hardware, and overhead.

body.text: Second, Quebec's Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations in Quebec (DICI) reduces the provincial corporate income tax rate on eligible intellectual property income from the general 11.5% provincial rate (which combines with the 15% federal rate for a 26.50% combined general corporate rate, versus the 12.20% combined small-business rate on the first $500,000 of active business income) down to an effective 2% provincial rate. Under the 2025–2026 Budget amendments, the calculation of the Québec nexus ratio for the DICI is explicitly not reduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold, ensuring that R&D expenditures below the $50,000 / employee basic personal amount floor still count in full toward the numerator of the corporation's Quebec nexus ratio. Furthermore, under the 2025–2026 Budget, corporations with assets under $50,000,000 recorded in their financial statements that were allocated an amount under the CRIC or one of the former R&D tax credits for a taxation year ended in 2025 or one of the three preceding taxation years preserve preferential qualification access.

Third, the Quebec Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation (C3i), administered by Revenu Québec for new manufacturing and processing equipment (CCA Classes 43 and 53), general-purpose computer hardware (Class 50), and qualifying management software packages (Class 12) acquired after March 10, 2020, and before January 1, 2030, is 100% refundable for expenses incurred in taxation years beginning after December 31, 2023. The C3i rate depends on the economic vitality of the territory where the equipment is mainly used (rather than the location of the head office): 15% inside the Montréal and Québec metropolitan communities, 20% in intermediate territories, and 25% in designated low economic vitality regional county municipalities. An exclusion threshold of $12,500 per property ($5,000 for computer hardware and management software) is subtracted before applying the credit rate, subject to a $100,000,000 cumulative cap across associated corporations (excluding unincorporated businesses, tax-exempt entities, Crown corporations, aluminium producers, and oil refiners). While a corporation can claim both the C3i and the CRIC in the same taxation year on different assets, the same capital asset cannot be double-claimed under both the C3i and the CRIC.
Summary of Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credits Across Canada

Outside Quebec, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits generally piggyback directly on the federal subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED and the qualified expenditure pool reported on Form T661, adding between 3.5% and 20% in sub-national tax relief. In Ontario, CCPCs claim the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) on up to $3,000,000 of eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (which phases out based on prior-year taxable income and taxable capital employed in Canada), alongside the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) available to all corporations on eligible SR&ED expenditures after deducting the OITC. In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides corporations that undertake R&D in Alberta with a refundable credit of up to 20%—structured as an 8% base payment on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures plus a 12% incremental payment on expenditures exceeding the corporation's two-year average base spend—phasing out for larger firms based on taxable capital. In British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland and Labrador, provincial SR&ED tax credits range from 10% to 15% (generally refundable for CCPCs in the western provinces and 100% refundable for all corporations in the Atlantic provinces), while the Yukon R&D Tax Credit provides a 15% fully refundable credit (plus an additional 5% on eligible payments made to Yukon University).

body.text: Administrative Governance, Filing Procedures, Penalties, and the 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Regime
Mandatory Forms, Schedules, and Electronic Filing

At the federal level, the SR&ED Tax Incentive Program is administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Corporate claimants must submit their SR&ED claim as an integrated component of their T2 Corporation Income Tax Return via Corporation Internet Filing using CRA-certified commercial tax software or through an EFILE-certified tax preparer transmitting on the corporation's behalf. (Taxpayers must note that NETFILE is an individual tax filing portal and cannot be used by corporations). Under subsection 150.1(2.1) of the Income Tax Act, electronic filing of the T2 return is mandatory for virtually all corporations regardless of gross revenue, and submitting a paper T2 return triggers an automatic $1,000 statutory penalty under subsection 162(7.2).

To constitute a valid filing, a corporate SR&ED submission must include three core prescribed forms and schedules. First, the taxpayer must complete Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) in accordance with Guide T4088 (Guide to Form T661). Form T661 is updated to reflect the Bill C-15 capital expenditure and expenditure limit rules and requires the claimant to report project-by-project technical narratives in Part 2, project-level costing, allowable SR&ED expenditures and the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in Parts 3 and 4, the Prescribed Proxy Amount calculation in Part 5, assistance repayments on Line 370 / Line 460, the Part 8 Claim Checklist, and Part 9 Claim Preparer Information. Every taxpayer incurring SR&ED expenditures must file Form T661 whether or not an Investment Tax Credit is claimed in the year. Second, corporate claimants must file Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations), which imports the qualified expenditure totals from Form T661 to compute the 35% enhanced and 15% basic SR&ED ITCs, claim cash refunds under Section 127.1, or apply carrybacks and carryforwards against Part I tax (while also coordinating with clean economy credits such as the Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC reported on Schedule T2SCH76 and Line 170 of Schedule 31). Third, where a CCPC is associated with one or more other CCPCs, the group must file Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.3).
The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Bar

One of the most rigid procedural rules in Canadian tax law is the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline codified in subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. Under these provisions, a taxpayer must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 containing all prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is exactly 6 months after the end of its taxation year (whereas its balance of tax payable is due 2 months after year-end under paragraph 157(1)(b), or 3 months after year-end for an eligible CCPC), a corporation's statutory deadline to file or amend an SR&ED claim is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year.

For example, a corporation whose taxation year ended on December 31, 2023, had a T2 filing-due date of June 30, 2024, and an absolute SR&ED filing deadline of June 30, 2025; similarly, a corporation with a fiscal year ending on December 31, 2025, has a T2 filing-due date of June 30, 2026, and an absolute SR&ED filing deadline of June 30, 2027. While a corporation that has already filed its T2 return on time at the 6-month mark is permitted to file an amended return adding Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 at any point up to the 18-month mark, there is no statutory mechanism in the Income Tax Act to extend or waive the 18-month deadline. Neither the Minister of National Revenue under the Taxpayer Relief Provisions nor the Tax Court of Canada possesses jurisdiction to accept a Form T661 filed even one day after the 18-month bar; any expenditures or credits not reported on prescribed forms by that date are permanently forfeited.
Part 9 Claim Preparer Disclosures and Subsection 162(5.1)–(5.2) Penalties

While there is no statutory requirement to hire an external consultant to file an SR&ED claim, many Canadian companies—particularly first-time claimants—engage specialized SR&ED advisory firms that typically charge contingency fees ranging from 15% to 25% of the refund amount. To combat aggressive contingent-fee claim padding and ensure regulatory oversight, Parliament enacted strict disclosure obligations in Part 9 (Claim preparer information) of Form T661, backed by statutory penalties under subsections 162(5.1) and 162(5.2) of the Income Tax Act.

In Part 9 of Form T661, the claimant corporation and every claim preparer who accepts consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the SR&ED claim must disclose the claim preparer's name and Business Number, specify the billing arrangement (contingency fee percentage, flat fee, or hourly rate), list the total fee paid or payable, and sign a joint certification (with administrative provisions enacted in 2014 allowing Part 9 to be filed separately where a claim preparer was involved after initial preparation). Even if no external claim preparer participated and the claim was prepared 100% in-house by the corporation's own employees, Part 9 must still be completed and signed to certify that no claim preparer was used. Under subsection 162(5.1), if any prescribed information regarding the claim preparer(s) in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty is assessed, and under subsection 162(5.2), the claim preparer and the claimant corporation are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable for paying that penalty.
April 1, 2026 Administrative Streamlining and Pre-Claim Technical Approval

Historically, the federal SR&ED program operated exclusively on a retrospective post-filing audit model: while approximately 90% of SR&ED claims are accepted as filed and processed within roughly 60 days, claims selected for a technical and financial review by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer (FR) required approximately 180 days for processing.

Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA implemented a major administrative modernization comprising two operational reforms. First, the CRA launched an elective Pre-Claim Approval Process, which allows eligible taxpayers to submit planned or ongoing R&D projects to the CRA for formal technical eligibility evaluation before significant R&D expenditures are incurred or before the corporate tax return is filed. By securing upfront technical validation that the project satisfies subsection 248(1), corporations gain immediate financing certainty and cut post-filing claim processing times in half—from 180 days down to 90 days. Second, the CRA deployed AI-based risk triage across incoming Form T661 filings, utilizing machine-learning models to fast-track low-risk claimants with clean compliance records while targeting manual audit resources toward claims exhibiting red flags such as generic marketing prose or unsupported cost allocations.
Jurisprudence, Audit Precedents, and Contemporaneous Documentation Standards
Judicial Interpretation of SR&ED: From Northwest Hydraulic to Jentel Manufacturing

The legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act is anchored by Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal jurisprudence. Building upon the foundational judicial criteria articulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839)—which established the Five Questions framework examining technological risk or uncertainty, hypothesis formulation, systematic adherence to the scientific method, technological advancement, and contemporaneous record-keeping—subsequent Tax Court decisions have strictly enforced the evidentiary threshold separating routine engineering from experimental development.

A landmark precedent demonstrating how the Tax Court of Canada adjudicates technological uncertainty is Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261 (Docket 2008-3875(IT)G, May 11, 2011), decided by Justice D'Arcy and affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355 (Docket A-222-11, December 15, 2011). In Jentel, the corporate appellant, which develops and manufactures engineered thermoformed plastic products, claimed SR&ED tax credits for its 2005 taxation year. Justice D'Arcy's ruling illustrates two points that guide CRA audit denials today. First, a record of contemporaneous work does not render a project eligible if genuine technological uncertainty is absent. Although the parties' agreed statement of facts recorded that contemporaneous records of the work were kept, the Court ruled that none of Jentel's activities qualified as SR&ED because the work involved using existing manufacturing processes and existing materials, and the taxpayer failed to prove a "technological risk or uncertainty" that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. The appeal was dismissed with costs.

Second, Justice D'Arcy applied the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as summarized by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, which ask, among other things, whether the claimant formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating the technological uncertainty and whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed. Because Jentel failed the threshold uncertainty criterion, its work could not qualify regardless of how it was recorded. On appeal, the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed Jentel's appeal with costs, holding that whether work constitutes SR&ED is a question of mixed fact and law and finding no error of law or palpable and overriding error in the trial judge's findings. Consequently, to survive Tax Court scrutiny and avoid characterization as "trial and error" engineering, a claimant's records must explicitly connect an identifiable hypothesis and potential designs to measured results from testing and experiments, and must show how subsequent modifications to original designs were logically derived from those measured test results.
Contemporaneous Documentation Standards and Part 2 Narrative Precision

Under paragraph 230(4)(b) of the Income Tax Act, every taxpayer must retain all books, accounting records, and supporting technical documentation for a minimum of six years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate. It is settled law and CRA administrative practice that the CRA will deny SR&ED expenditures and activities wherever a taxpayer fails to maintain clear, contemporaneous documentation generated as the R&D work progressed, rather than narratives reconstructed after the fact.

When drafting the three technical narrative sections of Part 2 of Form T661 (describing the technological advancement sought, the technological obstacles/uncertainties faced, and the systematic work performed to overcome them), domain experts adhere to three strict drafting rules. First, the narrative must name and quantify the baseline state of the art from which the team started: because technological uncertainty only exists relative to what was already publicly known, failing to specify the existing industry benchmark, standard libraries, or physical limits prevents the CRA reviewer from verifying the uncertainty. Second, the narrative must quantify every experimental iteration, including failed experiments: vague statements such as "we tried several approaches" are treated by CRA reviewers as an admission of routine trial and error, whereas stating "four architectural approaches were formulated and benchmarked against a fixed 10-million-record workload, with the first three ruled out due to measured memory-leak and latency data" proves a systematic investigation. Third, claimants must strike all marketing adjectives: terms such as "revolutionary", "cutting-edge", and "world-class" are flagged by CRA reviewers and AI triage models as noise or signals of claim-padding, and must be replaced with precise engineering metrics, software version numbers, and measured test outcomes.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions and Audit Readiness Recommendations

The enactment of federal Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 (retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024), the implementation of Quebec's 2025–2026 CRIC and CDAE-IA reforms, and the launch of the CRA's April 1, 2026 Pre-Claim Approval framework represent a generational expansion of non-dilutive R&D financing in Canada. To capture the full financial benefit of these statutory changes while insulating claims against CRA and Revenu Québec audit adjustments, corporate tax leaders and technical executives should immediately integrate five strategic protocols into their tax governance cycle.

First, corporations whose taxation years began after December 15, 2024, and remain within their 18-month statutory filing window under subsection 37(11) should conduct an immediate retroactive review of 2025 and 2026 filings. Specifically, CCPCs that capped their 35% enhanced claim at the old $3,000,000 limit or suffered phase-out reductions under the legacy $10,000,000–$50,000,000 taxable capital corridor, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations that previously claimed only the 15% non-refundable rate, and enterprises that acquired new R&D capital equipment (used ≥ 90% in SR&ED) after December 15, 2024, should file or amend Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 before their 18-month bar expires to recover up to $2,100,000 in annual refundable federal credits.

Second, venture-backed and capital-intensive CCPCs whose balance sheets exceed $15,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada—whether due to preferred equity rounds, convertible notes, or project debt—should model and execute the Revenue Method election under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32). Where an unassociated CCPC or an associated CCPC group has three-year average annual gross revenue below $15,000,000 (or lower than its taxable capital figure), filing the prescribed revenue election restores the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit; however, tax directors must ensure that every CCPC in an associated group joins the election and that Schedule T2SCH49 is filed on time to avoid a Ministerial allocation under subsection 127(10.4).

Third, corporations operating in Quebec must restructure their provincial tax compliance for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, by transitioning from the repealed R&D salary and university/consortium credits to Form RD-1029.8.CR under the CRIC. Accounting systems must be updated to capture newly eligible pre-commercialization validation, testing, and prototyping costs alongside R&D capital expenditures, while factoring in the standardized 50% subcontractor inclusion rate and the $50,000 / employee basic personal amount exclusion threshold. For Quebec software and industrial enterprises utilizing artificial intelligence after December 31, 2025, segregating AI/ML specialist payroll into the CDAE-IA (to capture the 30% credit above the $18,571 per-employee threshold) while routing non-AI developers, capital equipment, and overhead into federal SR&ED and the CRIC yields the highest net cash recovery.

Fourth, software, AI, and data analytics companies must enforce Day-1 SR&ED-aware bookkeeping and cloud resource tagging. By separating production hosting (COGS) from experimental R&D compute in AWS, GCP, and Azure via automated project tags, collecting contemporaneous monthly developer timesheets linked to Jira/Git repositories, and settling all accrued R&D bonuses for arm's-length staff within 180 days of fiscal year-end under subsection 78(4), claimants eliminate the primary triggers for financial audit disallowances.

Finally, for capital-intensive or technically novel R&D initiatives commencing in 2026 and beyond, claimants should actively utilize the CRA's April 1, 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process. Obtaining upfront technical sign-off from the CRA de-risks R&D capital allocation, satisfies external financial statement auditors, and cuts post-filing cash refund processing times from 180 days to 90 days.
